title: Children and loss
hook: Kisa Gotami's story, for parents who have lost a child, told gently
tomorrow: an old fridge-magnet verse about friends. does Buddhism have one?

segments.voice: Yesterday, playing: Ryokan in the field, a glad mind fully in the game. Today the family week ends on its hardest page, and we go slowly.

A gentle word first: today's story is about a child who dies. If that is your story too, take this slowly, or save it for another day. People who grieve often say the hardest part is what others say: everything happens for a reason, at least you can try again. A young mother named Kisa Gotami heard her own version. Her little boy died, and she couldn't accept it. She carried him on her hip from house to house, asking everyone for medicine. People shook their heads. One of them, kinder than the rest, said: go and ask the Buddha.
screen: `A GENTLE WORD FIRST.` → `EVERYTHING HAPPENS FOR A REASON.` → `FROM HOUSE TO HOUSE.` → `GO AND ASK THE BUDDHA.`

segments.voice: The story comes from the old commentaries, and her own verses are kept in the Therigatha, the songs of the early nuns. She reaches the Buddha and asks for medicine. He doesn't argue. He doesn't tell her to stop crying. He says yes: bring me a mustard seed, from a house where no one has died. So she goes door to door again, and this time something changes. Every family has a seed to give, and none can give it. A father was lost here. A daughter there. A husband. A grandmother, a baby brother. By evening she understands that her grief is not a strange, lonely thing. It lives in every house on the street. She lays her son down, gently, and goes back. The story is often told as a hard lesson: everyone dies, so let go. Read slowly, it's softer than that. The Buddha didn't send her away with an answer. He sent her to her neighbors, and at every door someone held her loss next to their own. Nobody hurried her. Nobody fixed it. For a parent who has lost a child, the tradition doesn't offer a reason. It offers company: held gently.
screen: `A MUSTARD SEED, PLEASE.` · `FROM A HOUSE WITH NO DEATH.` · `EVERY DOOR HAS LOST SOMEONE.` · `COMPANY, NOT A REASON.` · then, large: `HELD GENTLY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind parents who have lost a child: people you know, or people you'll never meet. Hold them the way the village held Kisa Gotami, without fixing anything, and silently offer: may you be held gently. If this loss is your own, let the wish turn toward you, and stay with it as long as you like.
Children and loss: Kisa Gotami's road from door to door, where grief turns out to live in every house.
A line to keep: held gently, by people who have lost too. Eleven of eleven; the family days are done.

howItsDone: Buddhists tell Kisa Gotami's story at funerals and in teaching on grief; families often hold memorial rites with monks or teachers and dedicate merit to the one who died.

chat.says: a couple brought in a tiny baby photo to frame. the baby died. i froze. what do you even say?
options: No perfect words. Say you're so sorry, take your time, and treat that frame with care.
Remind them everyone dies; that's the Buddha's lesson from the mustard seed story.
Say nothing about the baby. Bringing it up will only make their grief worse.
